title: Enhancing Dimension-Reduced Scatter Plots with Class and Feature Centroids
authors: Daniel B. Hier, Tayo Obafemi-Ajayi, Gayla R. Olbricht, Devin M. Burns, Sasha Petrenko, Donald C. Wunsch
text:
Big data and precision medicine initiatives are creating large datasets with numerous observations and many features [1,2]. In particular, genomic and molecular biological datasets are characterized by high dimensionality [3,4]. The goal of dimension reduction is to simplify the dataset by reducing the number of features while retaining as much of the original information as possible. Dimension reduction is especially important when dealing with high-dimensional data, where a large number of features can lead to complexity, increased computational costs, and the risk of overfitting by machine learning models [5,6,7].

High-dimensional datasets can be visualized as scatter plots when reduced to two dimensions. A variety of dimensionality reduction methods are available, including locally linear embedding (LLE), isometric feature mapping (ISOMAP), multidimensional scaling (MDS), uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), principal component analysis (PCA), and t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) [8,9,10,11,12,13]. These methods vary in stochasticity, linearity, sensitivity to parameter changes, and their ability to preserve the local and global structure of the data. The interpretation of scatter plots after dimension reduction remains complex. After dimension reduction, the x and y axes cannot be easily labeled and are typically expressed in arbitrary units that reflect the operations of complex algorithms [14].

We present a method to enhance the interpretability of two-dimensional scatter plots obtained after dimension reduction. Feature and class centroids are overlaid onto the plots to enhance interpretability. This approach addresses the challenge of interpreting the axes of dimension-reduced plots.

To demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, we used it to visualize the phenotypes of three rare neurogenetic diseases: hereditary spastic paraparesis (HSP), hereditary cerebellar ataxia (CA), and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT). Gene mutations cause all [15,16,17]. We sought to capture the phenotypic variability between these diseases with a scatter plot. Specifically, we reduced a high-dimensional space with 31 available phenotype categories (Fig. 1) to two dimensions and overlaid class and feature centroids. Before dimension reduction, the data had 31 columns (each column representing a phenotype feature) and 235 rows (each row representing a variant of either Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, cerebellar ataxia, or hereditary spastic paraparesis).

Relevant Prior Work. Reviews of dimension reduction methods for the visualization of high-dimensional datasets are available [18,12,19,8,13]. Based on quantitative benchmarks and end-user preferences, [20] found that t-SNE and UMAP outperformed other dimension reduction methods. UnProjection [21] is a project that uses neural networks to reconnect the low-dimension space to the high-dimension space. Interaxis is a project that allows end users to interactively manipulate the axes of low-dimensional scatter plots to explore the influence of features on the plotted positions of markers [22]. In similar work, Eckelt et al. [23] have suggested adding group centroids to low-dimensional embeddings of high-dimensional datasets. [24] has used annotations to make disease-phenotype plots based on t-SNE more interpretable. [25] have created t-viSNE as a visual interactive inspector of t-SNE scatter plots. It can generate interpretive feature bar charts based on the t-SNE plots that are the circumscribed areas of interest. [26] introduced NoLiES, an interactive system to improve the interpretability of low-dimensional embeddings by circumscribing rangesets on the plots.
